Hook.voiceover: A regulator asks you: why did you decide this system is not high-risk? If your answer is, it seemed fine, you have a problem. A classification is only as strong as the reasoning you can show later.

Explain.voiceover: So far, we have learned the Act's risk tiers and its roles. Today, we turn them into a repeatable method. This lesson is educational and is not legal advice, and every step must be checked against the official text of the EU AI Act.

slide.title: Classifying an AI System Step by Step
slide.body: Lesson 5 of 14. Footer line: Educational, not legal advice.

Explain.voiceover: The method has five steps. Work through them in order, and write down your answer and your reason at each step. Step one: describe the system and its purpose. What does it do, who uses it, who is affected, and what decisions does its output support? If the vendor's stated purpose and your actual use differ, record both.

slide.title: Step 1: Describe
slide.body: Five numbered boxes in a row, box 1 highlighted: What does it do? · Who uses it? · Who is affected? · What decisions does it support? · Vendor purpose vs actual use

Explain.voiceover: Step two: is it an AI system under the Act? The Act has its own definition, based on features such as working with some autonomy and inferring from inputs how to produce outputs like predictions, recommendations or decisions. Simple rule-based software may fall outside it.

slide.title: Step 2: Is it an AI system?
slide.body: Box 2 highlighted. Key features: some autonomy · infers from inputs · outputs predictions, content, recommendations or decisions. Side note: simple rule-based software may fall outside

Explain.voiceover: Step three: check the prohibited list. If there is a possible match, stop and escalate to legal counsel. Step four: check the high-risk categories. Is it a safety component of a regulated product, or used in a listed area such as employment or education?

slide.title: Steps 3 and 4
slide.body: Box 3 highlighted: prohibited list → possible match? STOP and escalate. Box 4 highlighted: safety component of regulated product? · listed area such as employment or education?

Explain.voiceover: Some systems in listed areas may not be treated as high-risk, for example if they only perform a narrow procedural task. That exception has conditions, so record exactly why you think it applies. Step five: check the transparency duties. These can apply in addition to high-risk duties.

slide.title: Step 4 exception and Step 5
slide.body: Under box 4: narrow-task exception, conditions apply, document why. Box 5 highlighted: transparency duties, can apply on top of high-risk duties

Explain.voiceover: Finish with a classification note. It records the tier, the reasoning at each step, the sources you used and their dates, your confidence, the reviewer's name and a date to review the decision again.

slide.title: The classification note
slide.body: Tier · Reasoning at each step · Sources and dates · Confidence · Reviewer · Next review date

Explain.voiceover: Think of a doctor's diagnosis checklist. A good doctor does not jump to a conclusion from one symptom. She goes through the same questions every time and writes down what she found. Another doctor can read the notes later and see exactly how she reached her decision.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's try it. Katrin Hoffmann is legal counsel at a fictional recruitment agency in Hamburg, Germany. The agency plans to use a CV-screening tool bought from a vendor.

Step one. The tool reads CVs, scores each one against a job description and produces a shortlist. Recruiters normally interview only the top twenty, so candidates are affected directly. Step two. The vendor says the tool uses a trained language model to infer match scores, so it is likely an AI system.

slide.title: Katrin's CV tool: steps 1 and 2
slide.body: 1. Scores CVs, produces shortlist; top 20 interviewed; candidates affected directly · 2. Trained language model infers scores → likely an AI system

Demonstrate.voiceover: Step three. It does not use emotion recognition or manipulative techniques, so there is no match with the prohibited list. Step four. Recruitment is a listed employment use, and the tool shapes who gets an interview, so the narrow-task exception does not seem to fit. It is likely high-risk, and the agency is a deployer.

slide.title: Katrin's CV tool: steps 3 and 4
slide.body: 3. No emotion recognition or manipulation → no prohibited match · 4. Employment use; shapes who is interviewed; exception does not fit → likely high-risk; agency = deployer

Demonstrate.voiceover: Step five. Candidates do not chat with the tool, but they must still be informed about its use under other rules, such as data protection law. Katrin's note says high-risk, deployer, confidence high. It lists her sources and sets a review date in six months, or earlier if the vendor changes the tool.

slide.title: Katrin's classification note
slide.body: Tier: likely high-risk · Role: deployer · Confidence: high · Sources: listed with dates · Review: in six months, or earlier if the vendor changes the tool

Demonstrate.voiceover: A common mistake is to classify once and never look again. If the agency starts using the tool to rank staff for promotion, or the vendor adds a feature that analyses facial expressions in video interviews, the answer may change. So write the review triggers into the note itself.

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, use five steps in order: describe the system, check the definition, check prohibited practices, check the high-risk categories, and check transparency duties. Second, write a classification note with reasoning, sources, confidence, reviewer and review date. Third, classification is not permanent. A new purpose or feature can change the tier.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Five steps, in order. 2. Write a classification note you can explain later. 3. New purpose or feature → classify again.

CTA.voiceover: In the exercise below this video, you will use the five steps on two fictional systems: a billing chatbot at a telecoms company in Belgium, and an exam-proctoring tool at a university in Italy. Write a short classification note for each, with at least one review trigger.

slide.title: Your exercise
slide.body: Billing chatbot · Belgium · Exam-proctoring tool · Italy · Five steps each · Classification note with review triggers · Use only the facts given · About 30 minutes

CTA.voiceover: That completes module one. In the next lesson, we move to data protection principles across the AI lifecycle. See you there.
